story.headline: US and Iran trade heaviest strikes in weeks
story.summary: US and Iran exchanged the biggest round of attacks in over a month, with US strikes on Iran's southern coast and Iranian missile salvos at US bases in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait and Iraq.
story.display_body: The United States and Iran fought their heaviest exchange in more than a month over the nights of Monday 31 August and Tuesday 1 September, with a second consecutive night of US bombing along Iran's southern coast and Iranian missile salvos at US bases across the Gulf, reported Wednesday 2 September. US Central Command (CENTCOM) said it struck dozens of military targets on the coast; Iran's foreign ministry said one of the strikes hit a house during a wedding in the town of Kuhestak, overlooking the Strait of Hormuz, killing at least four people and wounding more than 68, and Iranian state media (IRIB) put the total dead across the country at 18, figures that could not be independently verified. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC — Tehran's elite military branch) said it fired ballistic missiles and drones at US facilities in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait and the Kurdish city of Erbil in Iraq; Jordan's army said it intercepted 10 of 13 incoming missiles and Kuwait reported downing drones and missiles with no casualties, while Washington did not immediately confirm any hits. President Donald Trump told Fox News that Iran would be "totally wiped out" if it retaliated and posted that he liked the US "position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait" — a claim the same reporting undercuts, since the strait "remains under Iranian blockade." Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, speaking at a Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (a China- and Russia-led security bloc) summit in Bishkek, said Tehran would reciprocate only if the US returned to the June memorandum of understanding that had paused hostilities and expired on 17 August.
story.why: the war that opened on 28 February 2026 has settled into a "repeatable pattern" of flare-ups, as one analyst told Al Jazeera, rather than a resolved conflict — and with Hormuz, the chokepoint for roughly a fifth of the world's seaborne oil, still contested, each cycle carries the risk of a miscalculation that pulls in the Gulf states now being hit.

story.headline: EU summons Russian envoy over Leipzig drone
story.summary: Germany blamed Russia for a failed explosives-laden drone attack at Leipzig airport; the EU and France summoned Russian envoys.
story.display_body: Germany's government formally blamed Russia on Tuesday 1 September for a failed drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport last month, and the EU and France summoned Russian envoys in response on Wednesday 2 September. Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said in a joint press conference that Berlin had concluded Russia was behind the attempted strike, in which an explosives-laden drone was found at the airport — a major DHL cargo hub — in early August. EU foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas, meeting counterparts in Ireland (which holds the rotating EU presidency), called the incident something with "all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism" and said she had summoned Russia's ambassador in Brussels; French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said Paris had summoned the Russian chargé d'affaires and pressed for European-level sanctions on Russia's "shadow fleet" of tankers. Kallas added that the EU's next Russia sanctions package — some 1,600 listings tied to the war in Ukraine — was still being assembled and "maybe there is more to be added."
story.why: an attributed sabotage attempt on civilian aviation infrastructure inside Germany marks an escalation of the hybrid warfare Europe has accused Moscow of waging, and it lands as the bloc debates how far to go on sanctions and support for Ukraine.

story.headline: Nicaragua bars opposition from elections
story.summary: Nicaragua's parliament unanimously approved a constitutional reform barring opposition parties from elections and extending the presidential term to seven years.
story.display_body: Nicaragua's National Assembly unanimously approved a constitutional reform on Tuesday 1 September that bars opposition parties from elections and lengthens the presidential term from six to seven years. Meeting in an extraordinary session in León, the single-chamber parliament — wholly controlled by President Daniel Ortega's Sandinista National Liberation Front (FSLN) — wrote in language excluding from any ballot those deemed to have taken part in "coup acts," "treason," or requests for foreign military intervention. The change is largely symbolic in a country where opposition figures have already been jailed or exiled and independent media shut down; a 2025 constitution had already barred parties not sharing the FSLN's "ideological line" and pushed the legislative vote back a year to November 2027. Ortega, who turns 81 in November, cast the measure as protection against US interference, while critics say he and his wife and co-president Rosario Murillo — eight of whose nine children hold state posts — are building a "dynastic dictatorship."
story.why: it formalises the end of competitive elections in Nicaragua and deepens a standoff with Washington and the Organization of American States, which called in early August for action against Managua.

story.headline: Charlie Kirk suspect ordered to trial
story.summary: A Utah judge ruled that Tyler Robinson will stand trial for the September 2025 killing of Charlie Kirk; he pleaded not guilty and faces the death penalty.
story.display_body: A Utah judge ruled on Tuesday 1 September that Tyler Robinson, 23, must stand trial for the September 2025 assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, finding the prosecution had presented enough evidence at a preliminary hearing. Robinson, who prosecutors say shot Kirk in the neck at a university campus rally and could face the death penalty, pleaded not guilty after the bindover ruling (a judge's decision that a case has enough evidence to proceed to trial). The state pointed to messages in which the suspect allegedly confessed the killing to friends, while the defence sought mainly to cast doubt on the DNA analysis linking him to the weapon.
story.why: the ruling clears the way for a capital murder trial in one of the most politically charged US killings of the past year, nearly a year to the month after Kirk's death.

story.headline: Egypt bus crash kills at least 16
story.summary: A bus crash on the Dahab-Nuweiba road in Sinai killed at least 16 and injured 28.
story.display_body: A bus crash on the Dahab–Nuweiba road in Egypt's Sinai Peninsula killed at least 16 people and injured 28 on Wednesday morning, 2 September. The accident struck a stretch of Red Sea coast dotted with tourist resorts; it follows a road accident last month in the northeastern governorate of Ismailia that killed 18 and injured 30, part of a chronic road-safety toll in Egypt.

story.headline: GHI and Lausanne Cites face closure
story.summary: Free Romandy weeklies GHI and Lausanne Cites will cease publishing in December absent a buyer, threatening about 30 jobs.
story.display_body: The free weeklies GHI (Genève Home Informations) and Lausanne Cités will stop publishing in December unless a buyer is found, their director said on Wednesday 2 September, putting about 30 of the group's 36 permanent jobs at risk. Director Pascal Fleury told the Keystone-ATS news agency that the titles' advertising-based business model is "dead" as the ad market collapses, and that the group preferred to wind down now rather than face bankruptcy next year. He added that the linked distribution company had lost clients who, thanks to federal press-aid rules, now get cheaper rates from Swiss Post. The closures would follow the end of the print edition of the free daily "20 minutes," another blow to Romandy's local press.
story.why: GHI and Lausanne Cités are fixtures of Geneva and Lausanne civic life — free, locally distributed papers that carry municipal notices and neighbourhood news that larger titles skip — so their loss would thin the local-information layer for two of French-speaking Switzerland's biggest cities.

story.headline: Swiss appeal to multinationals slips
story.summary: A McKinsey/AmCham study says Switzerland remains attractive to large companies but faces intensifying international competition.
story.display_body: Switzerland remains an attractive base for large companies but is losing ground to intensifying international competition, according to a study by consultancy McKinsey and the Swiss-American Chamber of Commerce published Wednesday 2 September. The two authors — a management consultancy and a business lobby, whose remit is to argue for a lighter-touch, lower-cost environment for their members — frame the finding as a call for policy "action." The underlying claim is that the business environment is still favourable, not that firms are leaving; the "erosion" is relative, measured against other jurisdictions courting the same multinational headquarters.
story.why: studies of this kind feed directly into Swiss debates over corporate tax, regulation and the OECD minimum-tax rollout, so it is worth reading who is doing the measuring and what they are asking for before treating "declining attractiveness" as an established fact rather than an advocacy framing.
